hook.text: Massive objects bend light. A galaxy cluster can warp and magnify the image of objects behind it—a cosmic magnifying glass.

buildup.text: Einstein predicted this. Arthur Eddington confirmed it in 1919 by measuring starlight bent around the Sun during an eclipse.

discovery.text: Strong lensing creates arcs and multiple images. JWST has captured stunning lensed images of the most distant galaxies known.

twist.text: Lensing reveals invisible mass. The way light bends tells us exactly where dark matter is concentrated in a cluster.

climax.text: Weak lensing—subtle distortions across millions of galaxies—maps dark matter on the largest scales in the universe.

punchline.text: Gravity bends light around massive objects. The cosmos has its own telescope.

quiz.question: How does gravitational lensing help scientists study dark matter?
options: The way light bends reveals where invisible dark matter is concentrated
Dark matter emits lensed light that telescopes can detect
Lensing destroys dark matter, making it briefly visible

details.summary: Gravitational lensing occurs when massive objects like galaxies or galaxy clusters bend the path of light from background sources, acting as natural magnifying glasses.
details.whyItMatters: Gravitational lensing is the primary tool for mapping dark matter, which emits no light. It also magnifies the most distant galaxies, letting us study the early universe in detail otherwise impossible.
takeaways: Massive objects bend light paths through curved spacetime
Creates arcs, rings, and multiple images of background objects
Primary method for detecting and mapping dark matter

faq.question: What is an Einstein ring?
faq.answer: When a background source, a massive lens, and the observer are perfectly aligned, the source's light is bent equally in all directions, forming a complete circle — an Einstein ring. Perfect rings are rare, but partial arcs are common in galaxy cluster images.

faq.question: How does lensing reveal dark matter?
faq.answer: The amount of light bending reveals the total mass of the lens — including invisible dark matter. When astronomers compare the lensing-derived mass to the visible mass (stars and gas), the lensing mass is typically 5-10 times greater.
